short: Movable metal type made ideas cheap to copy and impossible to suppress.
full:
Johannes Gutenberg's press, developed at Mainz around 1440, combined several existing elements — a screw press, oil-based ink, and above all a hand mould for casting interchangeable metal type quickly and to a consistent height. Printing with movable type already existed in Korea and China; Gutenberg's contribution was a system suited to an alphabetic script and to industrial repetition.

Within fifty years there were printing shops in more than 250 European towns and perhaps twenty million volumes in circulation. The consequences were structural rather than merely convenient: standardised texts made cumulative scholarship possible, vernacular printing hardened national languages, and the Reformation spread at a speed no earlier heresy could match.
